To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

• Global atmospheric models with horizontal grid spacing of ~10 km or less, when coupled to the ocean, can simulate the global climate system at a level of accuracy that is adequate for many practical purposes.

1) the climate of Earth is highly sensitive to changes in the atmospheric concentration of greenhouse gases and aerosols and 2) this sensitivity can be quantified with confidence by using the best available global climate models.

(a) the global atmospheric circulation can be accurately simulated by a global atmospheric model with horizontal resolution as coarse as T21, and (b) a global atmospheric model can simulate the atmospheric circulation in the tropics, including the Madden-Julian Oscillation, only when the resolution is at least T42.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a comprehensive, fine-resolution, global atmospheric model, and its application to the study of climate and climate change.
the following questions: • How does the climate system respond to changes in forcing, and how does the response vary as a function of spatial scale and time?
understanding the physical processes that control the global climate and its variability, and how these processes are affected by the presence of human-induced perturbations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of fine-resolution global models has been of great benefit to the climate modeling community.
we are still in the process of understanding the climate system and its sensitivity to the forcing of anthropogenic greenhouse gases and aerosols.
the use of fine-resolution models in global climate research has not been as productive as it might have been.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results of the experiments we have done with the high-resolution models are consistent with the results from the lower resolution models, and that the high-resolution models do not show any significant differences that would change our understanding of climate.
we have been able to demonstrate that fine resolution models are capable of providing new insights into the dynamics and physics of the atmosphere.
we were the first to use a high-resolution global model for climate change research and to demonstrate the value of such models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the global climate system has many more degrees of freedom and weaker interactions among them than is generally assumed.
the climate of the Earth is not a smooth continuum but is a highly complex and heterogeneous mixture of processes that operate on a wide range of scales.
the atmosphere has a lot of structure and variability at scales that we can resolve with current models.
